A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' study of jailbreak transferability, despite the changed title. Text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including content moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments across 20 models, representation-similarity measurements, three distillation experiments, and passive and active jailbreak-transfer results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds AIM safety trajectories, attack-type analyses, and representation-similarity results across model layers.

M1.justification: The distillation procedure still combines teacher responses to benign Alpaca prompts with student refusal responses to AdvBench prompts. Representation measurement and the refusal-ablation-plus-GCG attack remain unchanged. The stronger benign-only framing does not establish a different training procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use Alpaca, AdvBench, and the same StrongREJECT coverage of 33 strategies applied to 313 harmful prompts. The new AIM and persona-versus-cipher analyses examine existing coverage; no new dataset, modality, or input scenario is established.

E2.justification: The same original-versus-distilled student comparisons, teacher–student pairs, and active attack are retained. The added analyses and related-work citations do not introduce a new competing attack or defense evaluated against the proposed procedure.

E3.justification: Appendix F adds reported similarity evaluations at layer fractions from 0.1 through 1.0, and Appendix E introduces attack-type coverage summaries at strength thresholds 0.3 and 0.5. Core response-generation settings, training budgets, and distillation hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds a refusal case study and an analysis of AIM vulnerability across distillation checkpoints using all 313 prompts. Appendices E and F add attack-type reliability and coverage analyses, a PCA visualization, and layer-sensitivity comparisons. These substantially expand the questions examined beyond v1's aggregate transfer analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix E newly specifies a Pearson correlation analysis between jailbreak strength and success. The ten-response sampling practice and score-range analysis are retained; no additional training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds AIM safety trajectories, attack-by-model heatmaps, and layer-specific similarity results. Appendix E newly reports, for example, 47% versus 8% model coverage for persona versus direct attacks at strength at least 0.3. The passive-transfer curves also show different intermediate trajectories in v1 Figure 4 and v2 Figure 5, without explaining whether measurements or plotting changed.

T1.justification: The strength, success, mutual-neighbor similarity, AUROC, and conditional transfer-mean definitions retain their mathematical meaning. Equation 6 replaces a finite average with equivalent expectation notation. No theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added.

C1.justification: The existing representation-alignment and distillation-transfer claims remain. However, the abstract and contributions add a substantial claim that persona attacks transfer through shared semantic representations while cipher attacks exploit model-specific quirks. The introduction also adds the claim that distillation can transfer safeguards and reduce vulnerability.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of distillation as transmitting both vulnerabilities and safeguards, explains attack-type differences through shared semantics versus idiosyncratic mechanisms, and distinguishes isolated successes from broad susceptibility. Section 5.2 additionally claims improvement without explicit safety fine-tuning, although Section 5 retains refusal examples in training. The original limitations and external-safeguard discussion are retained elsewhere.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and rationales for the representation-layer and neighbor-count choices. It omits v1's explicit GPT-4o-mini judge identity and AUROC success threshold of 0.5. Hardware, training hyperparameters, model identifiers, and the judging rubric remain; the rubric is relocated and its placeholders clarified.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to attack mechanisms, superposition, subliminal learning, and representation-space transfer through Kirch et al., Gorton and Lewis, Cloud et al., and Gupta et al.; Lad et al. supports layer selection. The Qwen2.5 technical-report and Zheng et al. judge citations disappear. The main related-work organization and foundational positioning remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, and measurement explanations are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries move to Appendix A, much of the discussion moves to Appendix C, and broader impacts become a main-text ethics statement. The distillation section gains separate transferability and safety subsections.

P2.justification: v2 replaces Figure 1 and adds distillation examples, AIM trajectories, attack-type heatmaps, PCA, and ten layer-specific similarity heatmaps. Existing figures gain family distinctions and teacher–student labels, and the variability histogram's axes are corrected. Tables and the judging template are also reformatted and relocated.

improvement.justification: The AIM trajectories and attack-type and layer analyses make the existing empirical findings more informative and inspectable, while restructuring and a code link improve usability. The net gain is limited: v2 removes two explicit evaluation settings, leaves changes to passive-transfer curves unexplained, and does not reconcile its claim of safety improvement without safety fine-tuning with the retained refusal-training mixture.
